title: Supreme (Sn 4.5)
hookLine: read it: calling your own view best
tomorrow: what's still yours from a dream, once you wake up?

lines: IT'S A POT! IT'S A POST!
cards: The men are hitting each other now. Fists, shoving, shouting over one another. It's a pot!
It's a post! It's a broom, you fool! A king watches, and he's delighted, because he set this up.

He had men who were born blind brought to an elephant, each one placed at a different part, and then asked each: what is an elephant like? So that's the cost of calling your view the best. Not just being wrong.

teach.h: THIS ALONE IS TRUE, THEY ARGUE.
teach.b: The story is in the Udana, and the Buddha tells it about teachers of his day who argued, this alone is true, everything else is worthless. The man at the head said a pot. The ear, a winnowing basket.
The leg, a post. The tail, a pestle. Each one touched something real.
The fight began when one part was called the whole. The fifth poem of the chapter of eights says the same thing without the elephant.

In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata: a person who settles into a view and calls it the highest in the world will call every other view inferior, and so never gets past quarrels. The skilled call that a knot.
Then the poem turns the light on the one doing the measuring.

teach.h: NOT EQUAL, NOT LOWER, NOT BETTER.
teach.b: Don't think of yourself as equal, it says, or lower, or better.
Hear that again. Not only don't think you're better. Don't think you're worse, either, or exactly even.
Drop the scale. And among people who are divided, don't take a side just to have one.
Not the best isn't false modesty. It's putting the ruler down.

how: The parable of the blind men and the elephant is told in Buddhist teaching on clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in other Indian traditions; the chapter of eights is studied for its teaching on letting go of views.

o: chosen by a teacher to lead the others
kind and gentle toward everyone you meet
highest of all, the top that makes others low

games.q: the elephant and the poem — tap the pairs.
p: the scale the poem sets down

s: the poem only warns against thinking you're better than others
it says don't think yourself equal, lower or better: drop the measuring.
in the story, each blind man described something he really touched
the fight came from calling one part the whole elephant.

games.q: two friends are arguing whether a movie was a masterpiece or trash, and both want you to pick a side. by the poem, what's the move?
o: don't take a side just to have one; ask what each of them saw.
pick whoever has the stronger arguments; that settles it.
tell them both they're wrong and give your own verdict.
games.why: among the divided, the poem's sage doesn't take a side just to have one. each friend is holding one part of the elephant.

practice: Look at one object near you, a mug, a shoe, a pillow. Notice how much of it you can't see from where you are: the bottom, the inside, the far side.
Turn it slowly in your hands, or in your mind, and let each new side count as part of the same thing.

wordCard.voice: Supreme: the highest. The poem's warning is about calling your own view supreme, which turns every other view into something lower, and you into a fighter.

orig.note: Pali: highest, supreme. The poem is the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta, the eight verses on the supreme.

carryVoice: Your line: not the best. Not the worst, either; just one side of the elephant. That's poem five.

sources.ref: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta: the blind men and the elephant)

drop.name: the chapter of eights, read whole
